name: Baicapil

angle.text: Baicapil is a branded cosmetic active in scalp serums aimed at thinning hair, with its name pointing to baicalin from skullcap. People use it hoping for less shedding and denser-looking hair, and no trial of the product itself was found.

summary: Baicalin-themed cosmetic hair active with no trial of its own found.
note: Little published evidence specific to the product.
currentQuick:
Baicapil is a branded ingredient sold in hair-loss serums, linked to baicalin, a plant flavonoid from skullcap.
It is named in a 2025 review of cosmeceutical hair actives; no dedicated human trial was found.
How it works: Baicalin has been studied for other effects in laboratory work; no mechanism for hair growth is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: No safety data specific to the product were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.
deepLead:
Baicapil is a branded cosmetic hair-care active marketed for scalp hair-loss serums. Its name suggests a baicalin-based ingredient, and baicalin is a flavone glycoside found in Scutellaria (skullcap) species.
A 2025 trichology review lists Baicapil among the topical actives it examines, and describes such ingredients as heavily promoted on social media. The sources reviewed contain no detail on Baicapil's composition, manufacturer or controlled trial results, so this article is brief.

name: Dihydroquercetin glucoside

angle.text: DHQG is one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used in serums by people with thinning hair. The component has not been studied on its own for hair, and the claims rest on Redensyl marketing data.

summary: A taxifolin derivative in Redensyl; no studies of it on its own.
note: Only tested within multi-ingredient products.
currentQuick:
DHQG is a sugar-linked form of taxifolin, a plant flavonoid. In marketing it is one half of the Redensyl hair-growth active.
No study of DHQG alone was found; small studies test finished serums.
How it works: Taxifolin has laboratory findings in unrelated areas; no hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Taxifolin is reported as non-mutagenic in bacterial tests; no human safety data for DHQG were found.
deepLead:
Dihydroquercetin glucoside (DHQG) is described in hair-care marketing as one of the two components of Redensyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active; the other is EGCG-glucoside. It is a glucoside of dihydroquercetin, also called taxifolin, a flavanonol found in Siberian larch, milk thistle and other plants.
The sources reviewed contain no clinical study of DHQG on its own. Redensyl-containing serums have been examined in small cosmetic studies, and a 2025 review discusses Redensyl among topical hair actives.

name: EGCG-glucoside

angle.text: EGCG-glucoside is the green-tea-derived partner of DHQG in Redensyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used for thinning hair. EGCG has wider research, and hair data on this component alone are lacking.

summary: Green-tea catechin derivative used in Redensyl; no hair data on the component alone.
note: Only lab enzyme data on the compound itself.
currentQuick:
EGCG-glucoside is a sugar-linked version of green tea's EGCG. It is named as one of two components in the Redensyl hair-growth ingredient.
The only study found on it examined a digestive enzyme in vitro, not hair.
How it works: No hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Oral EGCG at high intakes is linked to liver toxicity per EFSA; no safety data for the topical glucoside were found.
deepLead:
EGCG-glucoside (EGCG2) is a glucosylated form of epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), the main catechin of green tea. In hair-care marketing it is named as one of the two components of Redensyl, alongside dihydroquercetin glucoside.
Published work on EGCG-glucoside is chiefly biochemical. A 2012 in vitro study found that EGCG and its glucoside both inhibited the human intestinal enzyme maltase, with IC50 values of about 20 and 31.5 micromolar respectively. That study concerns diabetes-related enzymes, not hair.

name: Biochanin A

angle.text: Biochanin A is a red-clover phytoestrogen named as a component of Capixyl, a cosmetic hair-growth active used on thinning scalp hair. It has been studied for other purposes, and hair studies on the compound itself were not found.

summary: Red-clover isoflavone named in Capixyl; studied for other things, not hair.
note: Phytoestrogen; no hair trials found.
currentQuick:
Biochanin A is a phytoestrogen from red clover and legumes. Hair-care marketing lists it as a component of Capixyl.
No hair-specific human study was found; trials of red clover isoflavones address menopause and bone.
How it works: It binds estrogen receptors in laboratory assays and weakly inhibits an enzyme in vitro; no hair-growth mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: As a phytoestrogen it has hormone-receptor activity in lab work; no safety data for topical hair use were found.
deepLead:
Biochanin A is an O-methylated isoflavone, a plant phytoestrogen found in red clover, soy, alfalfa sprouts, peanuts and chickpea. In hair-care marketing, red clover-derived biochanin A is named as a component of Capixyl, a cosmetic peptide-and-isoflavone hair-growth active.
The sources reviewed contain no clinical study of biochanin A for hair. Research on red clover isoflavones concerns other conditions, such as menopausal symptoms and osteopenia, and a 2025 review lists Capixyl among topical hair actives.

name: Suvomipic

chain: Follicle stem cells switch to growth
angle.text: Suvomipic (PP405) is an experimental once-daily topical from Pelage Pharmaceuticals that hair-loss followers watch as a possible new regrowth option. It is in phase 2, with early results reported by the company.

summary: Pelage's once-daily topical pyruvate-carrier inhibitor for hair loss, in phase 2 with early company-reported results.
note: Investigational; not approved; early-phase data only.
currentQuick:
Suvomipic is an experimental scalp gel from Pelage Pharmaceuticals aimed at androgenetic hair loss. It is in phase 2 trials.
Preliminary phase 2a results reported 31% of men reaching 20% or greater hair density gain at eight weeks, with no placebo responders; the trial was mainly a safety study.
How it works: It inhibits the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, thought to shift hair follicle stem cells toward glycolysis and activation.
Risks and caveats: Investigational and unapproved; safety data are early-phase. Phase 3 trials were planned for 2026.
deepLead:
Suvomipic (developmental code PP405) is an experimental topical drug for hair loss developed by Pelage Pharmaceuticals, a company spun out of UCLA in 2018. It is described as a possible first-in-class compound that inhibits the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC1 and MPC2), which is thought to raise pyruvate and push hair follicle stem cells toward glycolysis and growth.
It is formulated as a 0.05% scalp gel applied once daily. In preliminary phase 2a results released in June 2025, 31% of men with advanced baldness had a hair density increase of 20% or more at eight weeks, versus none of the placebo group; the trial was designed mainly to assess safety. It is not approved anywhere.

name: Quercitrin

angle.text: Quercitrin is a plant flavonoid sometimes floated in hair-health discussions for its antioxidant properties. Antioxidant lab data exist, and hair studies in people were not found.

summary: A plant flavonoid glycoside sometimes floated for hair, with antioxidant lab data but no hair studies in people.
note: No human hair-growth studies exist.
currentQuick:
Quercitrin is a flavonoid found in buckwheat, oak and some herbal extracts. It is discussed as a possible hair-supportive plant compound because of its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies.
No published human trial has tested it for hair growth, so its appearance benefit is unproven.
How it works: In animal and cell studies it is broken down to quercetin and dampens inflammatory signalling such as NF-kappaB and iNOS. None of this has been shown in hair follicles.
Risks and caveats: Safety for hair use has not been studied. Dietary exposure through plant foods is common; concentrated topical or supplement use has no published hair-related safety data.
deepLead:
Quercitrin (quercetin 3-rhamnoside, also called thujin) is a flavonoid glycoside in which the flavonol quercetin is bound to the sugar rhamnose . It occurs in plants such as Tartary buckwheat and several oak species, and in the dye quercitron .
It is listed in hair-care discussions as a plant flavonoid with possible hair-growth relevance. Published research on quercitrin itself concerns antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cells and animal models, mainly in the gut and in immune cells . No published human study has tested quercitrin for hair growth or hair loss.

name: Horsetail extract

angle.text: Horsetail extract is sold in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a silica source, with users hoping for stronger, fuller hair. Lab data are limited and single-ingredient hair trials were not found.

summary: A silica-rich herbal extract sold for hair and nails, with limited lab data and no single-ingredient hair trials.
note: Plant is toxic to livestock; human hair evidence is lacking.
currentQuick:
Horsetail extract comes from a fern-like plant and is promoted in hair supplements and shampoos for its silica content. Its folk use includes strengthening nails.
No human trial of horsetail alone has shown a hair benefit, so its appearance effect is unproven.
How it works: Lab studies show anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in cells. A silica-to-hair pathway is the usual proposal but has not been tested in published human trials.
Risks and caveats: The plant is toxic to livestock and may form nicotine in polluted conditions. Human safety data for hair-focused use are limited.
deepLead:
Horsetail extract is prepared from Equisetum arvense (field or common horsetail), a perennial non-flowering plant native to northern temperate regions . It is marketed in hair and nail supplements and shampoos as a source of silica, with the plant reported to contain silicon along with flavonoids, saponins, tannins and minerals .
Wikipedia describes evidence for its medicinal properties as limited, with laboratory data suggesting anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antimicrobial activity . No published human trial reviewed here has shown an effect of horsetail alone on hair growth, though at least two registered trials have tested multi-ingredient hair supplements .

name: Isoflavones

angle.text: Soy isoflavones such as genistein and daidzein come up in hair discussions because of their estrogen-like activity, with some users hoping for less thinning. They have been studied in people for other conditions rather than for hair.

summary: Soy-derived phytoestrogens discussed for hair, but studied in people for other conditions, not hair.
note: No hair-specific human studies found.
currentQuick:
Isoflavones are estrogen-like compounds from soy and other legumes. They are sometimes proposed as a food or supplement route to better hair.
Human research covers cancer, bone, menopause and skin, not hair, so the hair benefit is unproven.
How it works: They bind estrogen receptors weakly and are processed by gut bacteria, partly into equol. Any effect on hair follicles has not been demonstrated.
Risks and caveats: Long-term supplement safety data are described as insufficient. EFSA found no adverse effects in postmenopausal women up to 150 mg per day, with data gaps noted.
deepLead:
Isoflavones are plant compounds, concentrated in soybeans and other legumes, that act as phytoestrogens, meaning they have estrogen-like activity in mammals . The major soy isoflavones are genistein and daidzein, and daidzein can be converted by gut bacteria to equol .
They are discussed in hair circles as a dietary or topical way to influence hair through estrogen-receptor signalling or antioxidant effects. Wikipedia states that evidence for proven health benefits is limited, and its isoflavone article does not discuss hair . No hair-specific clinical study was found among the sources reviewed.

name: Estrogen topical for hair

angle.text: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol sold in Germany and parts of Latin America, are used for pattern hair loss to slow thinning. Trials suggest benefit in some regions of the scalp, and regrowth has not been shown.

summary: Scalp estrogen solutions, mainly alfatradiol, that may slow thinning in some regions but are not shown to regrow hair.
note: Not widely approved; label advises against use in pregnancy and under 18.
currentQuick:
Topical estrogen for hair usually means alfatradiol, a weak estrogen scalp solution sold in some countries for pattern hair loss.
Reports describe it slowing or stabilizing loss rather than thickening hair, and minoxidil outperformed it in a women's study.
How it works: Alfatradiol binds estrogen receptors weakly and inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing conversion of testosterone to DHT.
Risks and caveats: Scalp irritation from the alcohol vehicle and more oil production are reported. Safety in pregnancy and minors is unknown.
deepLead:
Topical estrogen for hair refers to estrogenic solutions applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss. The best-documented example is alfatradiol (17-alpha-estradiol), a weak estrogen and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as an ethanol-based scalp solution in Germany and some Latin American countries under names such as Ell-Cranell Alpha .
Wikipedia reports that alfatradiol slowed or stabilized hair loss in studies without increasing hair density or thickness, and that minoxidil outperformed it in a 103-woman study . More generally, estrogen is associated with thicker hair during pregnancy, and estradiol has documented skin effects, but its role as a hair-loss treatment is not established in the general sources reviewed .

name: Triamcinolone injections

angle.text: Dermatologists inject triamcinolone into patches of alopecia areata to regrow hair, and most treated patients have reported regrowth. It treats an autoimmune condition and is not used for ordinary pattern hair loss.

summary: A clinician-administered steroid injection for patchy alopecia areata, with reported regrowth in most treated patients.
note: Prescription-only, administered by clinicians.
currentQuick:
Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid that dermatologists inject into patches of alopecia areata to calm the immune attack on follicles.
A 2020 systematic review reported over half regrowth in about 81 percent of patients, though hair often regrows spontaneously in patchy disease.
How it works: It is a potent glucocorticoid, about five times as potent as cortisol, that suppresses local inflammation.
Risks and caveats: It is prescription-only. Documented effects vary by site; eye-injection use has caused raised eye pressure and endophthalmitis cases. Skin thinning is commonly described for skin injections.
deepLead:
Triamcinolone acetonide is a synthetic glucocorticoid, about five times as potent as cortisol, sold under brand names such as Kenalog . Injected into the skin (intralesional), it is used for inflammatory skin conditions and keloid scars, and dermatologists also use it for patchy alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair-loss condition .
A 2020 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found that about 81 percent of patients receiving 5 mg/mL triamcinolone injections achieved more than half regrowth . Wikipedia also cautions that hair often regrows spontaneously in patchy disease, making treatment effects hard to judge . The article is limited to appearance-relevant hair use; many other injection sites are medical uses unrelated to looks.

name: Deuruxolitinib

angle.text: Deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) is an oral drug approved in the US for severe alopecia areata, and people with extensive hair loss follow it for full regrowth. Trials showed strong regrowth, and it is not indicated for pattern baldness.

summary: Newly approved oral JAK inhibitor for severe alopecia areata, with strong regrowth data and a boxed warning.
note: Prescription drug with boxed warning (infections, cardiovascular events, thrombosis, malignancy); indicated for alopecia areata, not pattern baldness.
currentQuick:
Deuruxolitinib (Leqselvi) is an oral prescription pill approved in the US for adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of hair loss.
In a Phase 3 trial, adults with at least half of their scalp hair lost regrew significantly more hair on the drug than on placebo. It is not approved for male or female pattern hair loss.
How it works: It blocks Janus kinase enzymes, which relay inflammatory signals; this is thought to reduce the immune attack on hair follicles.
Risks and caveats: The label has a boxed warning for serious infections, death, cancer, heart events and blood clots. Common effects include headache, acne and raised cholesterol. It is contraindicated with certain CYP2C9 conditions and may harm a fetus.
deepLead:
Deuruxolitinib (brand name Leqselvi; formerly CTP-543) is an oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor approved in the United States for adults with severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy to total scalp and body hair loss. It is a deuterated form of a JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, and in vitro assays reported in the US label showed greater inhibitory potency for JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 than for JAK3.
Its efficacy was tested in the Phase 3 THRIVE-AA1 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults aged 18 to 65 with at least 50 percent scalp hair loss, which was published in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in 2024. Systematic reviews of JAK inhibitors in alopecia areata describe the class as producing meaningful regrowth while raising safety questions that include infections, acne and laboratory changes.
The US label carries a boxed warning covering serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis. The drug is a prescription medicine for a medical condition; discussion of it in appearance communities is tied mainly to hair regrowth in alopecia areata rather than to pattern hair loss.

name: Ruxolitinib oral

angle.text: Oral ruxolitinib is approved for blood and transplant conditions and is investigational for alopecia areata, where it is followed as an off-label route to regrowth. Hair evidence comes from smaller studies.

summary: Oral JAK inhibitor approved for blood and transplant disorders, only investigational for alopecia areata.
note: Systemic immunosuppressive prescription drug; not approved for hair loss.
currentQuick:
Oral ruxolitinib (Jakafi) is a prescription JAK inhibitor approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and graft-versus-host disease.
Alopecia areata is described as an area of investigation, but the sources reviewed here contain no results for it. Other JAK inhibitors have approvals or trial data in that condition.
How it works: It blocks JAK1 and JAK2 enzymes that relay cytokine signals inside immune cells.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include low blood counts, infections including shingles, raised cholesterol and liver enzymes. Reviews discuss cancer and infection concerns for the JAK inhibitor class. Prescription only.
deepLead:
Ruxolitinib is a Janus kinase (JAK1/JAK2) inhibitor developed by Incyte and sold orally as Jakafi in the United States and Jakavi elsewhere (Novartis). Its approved oral indications are blood and transplant conditions, namely myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera and graft-versus-host disease; a topical cream (Opzelura) is approved for atopic dermatitis and vitiligo.
Oral ruxolitinib is not approved for alopecia areata. It is discussed in hair-loss contexts because JAK inhibitors as a class have been studied for that autoimmune condition, and Wikipedia lists alopecia areata only as an area under investigation.
Because it is a systemic immunomodulating drug, reviews of JAK inhibitors in dermatology discuss infection and cancer risks for the class.

name: Methotrexate for alopecia

angle.text: Methotrexate is tried off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids, to regrow hair lost to autoimmune attack. Small studies and a 2019 meta-analysis exist, with definitive evidence described as scarce.

summary: Old immunosuppressant tried off-label for alopecia areata, supported by small studies and a meta-analysis.
note: Systemic immunosuppressant requiring medical monitoring; reports of raised liver enzymes with scalp delivery.
currentQuick:
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant sometimes prescribed off-label for alopecia areata, alone or with corticosteroids.
A 2019 meta-analysis noted limited definitive evidence; most data come from small or retrospective studies. Newer JAK inhibitors are now compared against it in trials.
How it works: It suppresses immune activity, which is thought to be relevant because alopecia areata is autoimmune.
Risks and caveats: It is a systemic prescription drug; a report found raised liver enzymes after scalp delivery sessions. Requires medical supervision.
deepLead:
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used in several skin diseases that has been tried off-label for alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss condition, either alone or alongside corticosteroids. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis described a paucity of definitive evidence and guidelines for this use.
Evidence consists mainly of small studies, case series and retrospective cohorts. Registered trials have compared it with newer agents such as tofacitinib and with other treatments.

name: Mometasone

angle.text: Mometasone is a steroid used for allergies, asthma and eczema, and it comes up in hair discussions through scalp inflammation and relatives used in alopecia areata. Hair-loss studies of it were not found.

summary: Potent steroid for allergies, asthma and eczema, with no hair-loss studies found.
note: Corticosteroid; topical use on skin is typically short term due to thinning risk.
currentQuick:
Mometasone furoate is a corticosteroid used in nasal sprays, inhalers and skin creams for allergy, asthma and eczema.
Although topical steroids as a class are associated with alopecia areata care, the sources reviewed here include no hair-loss data for mometasone itself.
How it works: It binds glucocorticoid receptors and dampens inflammatory signaling.
Risks and caveats: Risks listed include local infections, adrenal suppression with heavy exposure, skin thinning with prolonged topical use and fetal risk in animal studies.
deepLead:
Mometasone furoate is a synthetic glucocorticoid used in nasal, inhaled and topical forms for allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, asthma and inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema and psoriasis. Brand names include Nasonex, Asmanex and, for the topical form, Elocon.
The wiki lists it because topical corticosteroids are among treatments associated with alopecia areata. The sources reviewed for this article describe mometasone's approved uses and safety but contain no study of mometasone for hair loss, so evidence for that use is not documented here.

name: Diaminopyrimidine oxide

angle.text: Diaminopyrimidine oxide appears in hair-growth lotions and shampoos as a minoxidil-related cosmetic ingredient for people with thinning hair. It is known mainly from cosmetic patents, and trials were not found.

summary: Minoxidil-like cosmetic ingredient in hair lotions, known mostly from patents and with no trials found.
note: Source base is thin: patents and one broad review.
currentQuick:
Diaminopyrimidine oxide is an ingredient in some hair-growth lotions, described as minoxidil-like.
Sources reviewed are mainly cosmetic patents; no trials testing it were found.
How it works: Patents say such compositions enhance hair root activity; no mechanism data were found.
Risks and caveats: No safety data were found in the reviewed sources.
deepLead:
Diaminopyrimidine oxide is a minoxidil-related ingredient that appears in some hair-growth and anti-hair-loss lotions and shampoos. In the sources reviewed, it appears mainly in cosmetic patents, including Korean patent filings from 2007 and 2008 describing compositions of pyrrolidinyl diaminopyrimidine oxide for hair growth and for preventing hair loss.
A 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis compared off-label and unregulated therapies for male androgenetic alopecia beyond minoxidil. No randomized clinical trial of diaminopyrimidine oxide was found in the reviewed sources.

name: Sarcosine (hair)

chain: Follicle energy and cell support claimed
angle.text: Sarcosine is listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle cells. Hair studies behind it were not found.

summary: A glycine-derived amino acid listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with no hair studies behind it.
note: No hair-specific studies found; sourcing here is thin.
currentQuick:
Sarcosine is a small naturally occurring amino acid, an N-methyl form of glycine. It appears in discussion of hair-growth blends as one listed component.
No clinical study found tests it for hair growth, so its role in these products is unproven.
How it works: In the body it is an intermediate in choline-to-glycine metabolism. Any mechanism for hair effects has not been established in published research.
Risks and caveats: Sources reviewed describe no hair-specific safety data. Its sarcosinate derivatives are widely used as surfactants in consumer products.
deepLead:
Sarcosine, also called N-methylglycine, is a non-proteinogenic amino acid that is the N-methyl derivative of glycine. It occurs naturally in muscle and other tissues as an intermediate in the conversion of choline to glycine.
In appearance-related discussion it is mentioned as an ingredient in hair-growth blends. No published human study found in the sources reviewed has tested sarcosine itself as a hair-growth ingredient, so evidence for that use is unproven.

name: Cinnamomum zeylanicum bark extract

chain: Ceylon cinnamon bark in a blend
angle.text: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract appears in the cosmetic blend Sepicontrol A5 and is mentioned in hair-care product discussions. No hair or scalp studies were found for it.

summary: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract, listed in a cosmetic blend, with no hair or scalp studies behind it.
note: Evidence is limited to non-cosmetic lab and rodent work.
currentQuick:
This is an extract of the inner bark of the Ceylon cinnamon tree, described as one component of the Sepicontrol A5 cosmetic blend.
Published work on it covers memory in rodents and lab antioxidant tests; none addresses hair or scalp appearance.
How it works: No mechanism for hair or scalp effects has been established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Sources reviewed give no hair-specific safety data.
deepLead:
Cinnamomum zeylanicum is an older botanical name for Cinnamomum verum, the evergreen tree of Sri Lanka known as true or Ceylon cinnamon. Its dried inner bark is the cinnamon spice. Extracts of the bark are described as a component of Sepicontrol A5, a cosmetic ingredient blend.
Published research on the extract concerns non-cosmetic topics such as memory in rodents and in-vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activity. No study found tests it for hair or scalp appearance.

name: Hydroxypropyl ammonium gluconate

angle.text: This gluconate salt is paired with a gluconamide in bond-building hair products promoted for strengthening fibres and reducing breakage. The only research found is crystal chemistry, and the mechanism on hair was described as unknown.

summary: A gluconate humectant paired with a gluconamide in bond-building hair products; only crystal-chemistry research exists.
note: No human studies found.
currentQuick:
This gluconate salt is used alongside a gluconamide in a hair care mixture described as strengthening hair fibres.
The only published work found is a lab structural study; no human trial exists.
How it works: The 2022 paper said how the mixture acts on hair was unknown and studied its interactions with amino acids by crystallography.
Risks and caveats: No hair-specific safety data found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
3-Hydroxypropyl ammonium gluconate is a gluconate salt used with a gluconamide derivative in a hair care mixture that is described as strengthening hair fibres. A 2022 crystallography paper states that the mechanism of that mixture on hair was unknown and examined how the gluconamide and gluconate interact with amino acids.
The entry is described in hair-care discussion as a humectant in bond-building products. Gluconates are salts of gluconic acid, which occurs in fruit, honey and wine.

name: Hydrolyzed silk protein

angle.text: Hydrolyzed silk protein is added to conditioners so hair feels softer and looks glossier after use. Hair trials of the ingredient were not found.

summary: Broken-down silk protein used as a conditioning ingredient; no hair trials found.
note: Evidence limited to patents and unrelated animal work.
currentQuick:
Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk split into smaller peptides, found in conditioners and cleansers.
No human study found tests it for hair appearance.
How it works: Silk is mostly fibroin and sericin; hydrolysis makes smaller fragments. No hair mechanism is established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: No hair-specific safety data found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk protein broken into smaller peptides and amino acids, used in cosmetic products including hair conditioners. Silk is mainly fibroin with a coating of sericin.
Cosmetic formulations containing it appear in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions. No clinical trial found tests it for hair appearance.

name: Hydrolyzed keratin

angle.text: Hydrolyzed keratin is added to conditioners and repair products to strengthen and smooth damaged hair for a healthier look. Hair-specific human data are scarce.

summary: Broken-down keratin protein added to conditioners; marketed for repair, with almost no hair-specific human data.
note: Hair-benefit claims rest mostly on manufacturer positioning; one completed trial has no posted results.
currentQuick:
Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin protein, from sources such as feathers or wool, chopped into small fragments so it dissolves in water. It is added to conditioners and masks with claims of strengthening damaged hair.
A 120-person trial of a keratin peptide powder for hair health is registered as completed, but no results are posted. Most other published work is on non-cosmetic biomaterials.
How it works: Proponents say small protein fragments can deposit on or fill gaps in damaged hair. The sources reviewed here do not include studies testing that mechanism in hair.
Risks and caveats: No hair-specific safety findings are described in the sources reviewed. It is an ordinary cosmetic ingredient; individual products vary.
deepLead:
Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin, the structural protein of hair, wool, nails and feathers, that has been broken down into smaller peptide and amino-acid fragments so that it can dissolve in water. It is used as a protein ingredient in hair conditioners and similar products, where it is marketed for strengthening and repairing damaged hair.
Native keratin is highly insoluble, largely because of disulfide bonds formed by the amino acid cysteine, and only certain reducing or dissolving agents can break it down. Hydrolyzed forms are made from sources such as feathers and wool and have also been studied as biomaterials for tissue engineering, films and nanofibres.
Published evidence for cosmetic hair benefits is thin. A registered trial of a hydrolyzed keratin peptide powder for hair health has been completed, but its results are not described in the registry record.
